svg.title: Carbon & nanoparticles
svg.desc: Diamond: Each carbon bonds to four others in a rigid giant covalent network. Many strong bonds → very hard, high melting. No delocalised electrons or moving ions → does not conduct electricity. Useful for cutting. Graphite & graphene: Graphite: each carbon bonds to three others in hexagonal layers. One electron per carbon is delocalised → conducts. Weak forces between layers → slide → lubricant. Strong bonds within layers → high melting. Graphene: a single layer; very strong and conducting, useful in composites/electronics. Fullerenes & nanotubes: Fullerenes are hollow carbon cages/tubes, based on hexagonal rings; some also have five- or seven-sided rings. C₆₀ is a cage. Large surface area: catalysts. Hollow cages: drug delivery. Cylindrical nanotubes: high tensile strength and conductivity → composites/electronics. Size classes: Nanoparticles: 1–100 nm. Fine particles: 100–2,500 nm. Coarse particles: 2,500–10,000 nm. 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m. Smaller size increases surface area compared with volume; properties may differ from bulk material. Calculate the ratio: Cube of side x: area = 6x²; volume = x³; SA/V = 6/x. Use the same length units. Side 10 nm → SA/V 0.6 nm⁻¹; side 5 nm → 1.2 nm⁻¹. Halving size doubles the ratio. More exposed surface per amount → less catalyst/coating may be needed. Benefits & risks: Uses: catalysts, medicine, electronics, sunscreen and antibacterial coatings. Link each use to a useful property. Small particles may enter the body; effects depend on material, dose and exposure route. Compare benefit with toxicity/environmental evidence and uncertainties; do not assume all nanoparticles are safe or harmful.

g.text: Layers can slide past each other
